data.body:
OSS RESEARCH — LOCAL CONTENTION HANDLING IN MATURE PROJECTS (commissioned 2026-07-31)

>>> CORRECTION BY THE COORDINATOR, READ FIRST <<<
The report's "Grounding note" claims commit 5ef138d26 (the 304e boot-id fix) is NOT reachable from
main and that lock.py still carries the pre-fix `_owner_stamp()`. THAT IS WRONG. The researcher
measured against a STALE LOCAL CHECKOUT (HEAD 2a3abe6ab) instead of origin/main. Verified by me:
`git merge-base --is-ancestor 5ef138d26 origin/main` => TRUE; origin/main's _store/lock.py contains
the v2 stamp (`rebar-lock v2 host=... ns=... pid=... start=...`, _STAMP_V2_PREFIX at :177).
CONSEQUENCE: priority item #2 in section 5d ("Land fix-304e-container-lock on main") is ALREADY DONE
— ignore it. Everything else in the report stands. (This is the same stale-worktree trap that bit me
earlier tonight: always read `git show origin/main:<path>`, never the working tree.)

Every section separates CITED (a URL backs it) from EXTRAPOLATION (inference).

== 1. LOCAL GIT CONTENTION (index.lock / HEAD.lock / packed-refs.lock) ==

1a. What git gives you — CITED. Git HAS retry-with-backoff and deliberately does NOT use it for the
index. Generic path `lock_file_timeout()` in lockfile.c: quadratic backoff (multiplier += 2n+1, cap
BACKOFF_MAX_MULTIPLIER 1000, base INITIAL_BACKOFF_MS 1) with EXPLICIT JITTER —
`wait_ms = (750 + rand() % 500) * backoff_ms / 1000`, commented "back off for between 0.75*backoff_ms
and 1.25*backoff_ms". Retries only on EEXIST. timeout_ms==0 => one attempt; -1 => forever.
THE INDEX TAKES THE ZERO-TIMEOUT PATH: repo_hold_locked_index() takes no timeout and calls
repo_hold_lock_file_for_update(), the wrapper passing timeout_ms=0 (repository.c L471-478,
lockfile.h L223-230). So .git/index.lock = one attempt, no retry, NO CONFIG KNOB.
The three knobs that exist (Documentation/config/core.adoc L580-598): core.filesRefLockTimeout
(default 100ms), core.packedRefsTimeout (default 1000ms), core.configLockTimeout (default 1000ms).
0 = no retry, -1 = indefinite. No index equivalent.
Why refs got retry: Michael Haggerty's thread "Retry acquiring reference locks for 100ms" —
pack-refs and reflog expire lock refs WITHOUT changing their values, so retry has a real chance;
GitHub saw ~10-50 such errors/day fleet-wide (~1 in a million updates), near-zero after retry.
Jeff King argued packed-refs needs a longer timeout since it is O(number of refs). The thread never
discusses an index.lock equivalent.
New on git master (post-2025): core.lockfilePid writes a sibling foo~pid.lock containing "pid <n>",
PURELY DIAGNOSTIC. On failed acquire, unable_to_lock_message() probes kill(pid,0) and emits an honest
hedge: "if no git process is running, the lock file may be stale (PIDs can be reused)". Adds
diagnosis, not retry.
EXTRAPOLATION: found no message explicitly REJECTING an index-lock timeout knob; the absence is
evidenced by source/docs, not a stated decision. Plausible reason: index.lock is held across
arbitrary user work (conflicted merge, interactive add) where "wait longer" is not a meaningful bet,
whereas ref locks are held for microseconds by maintenance.

1b. Do tools set the knobs? — CITED. YES, the largest one does. Gitaly forces both globally on every
git invocation, reasoning inline (internal/git/gitcmd/command_factory.go L752-763):
  "Git has a default timeout of 1 second to try and lock the file. In practice though we see that
   this is not sufficient, and especially the DeleteRefs RPC is erroring out very frequently. We thus
   increase the timeout to 10 seconds. While comparatively high, context cancellation would still
   cause us to exit early in case the caller doesn't want to wait this long."
  core.packedRefsTimeout = 10000; core.filesRefLockTimeout = 1000 ("we have still observed lock
  contention around them though, but mostly in cases where the host system was heavily loaded by a
  storm of incoming RPCs"). Driving issue: gitaly#5160.
EXTRAPOLATION: outside Gitaly this appears rare — no other project found doing it. It is cheap
(`git -c core.packedRefsTimeout=...`) and UNDER-USED.

1c. The four mitigations — CITED.
  (a) Retry with jittered backoff: git lockfile.c; JGit RETRY_SLEEP_MS = [0,100,200,400,800,1600]
      ~3.1s for packed-refs (RefDirectory.java); lazygit 5x50ms then forcible unlink (commit 718e6d3).
  (b) Serialize behind your own lock: JGit holds a FAIR in-process ReentrantLock
      (inProcessPackedRefsLock = new ReentrantLock(true)) BEFORE touching the file lock; git-annex's
      joeyh fixed a user's index.lock failures by "only allow one git queue to be flushed at a time".
  (c) GIT_INDEX_FILE / worktree isolation: git-annex withIndexFile -> .git/annex/index
      (Git/Index.hs, Annex/GitOverlay.hs); GIT ITSELF does it in `git stash`
      (GIT_INDEX_FILE=$stash_index_path, builtin/stash.c) and git-filter-branch.sh L286-287.
      GOTCHA git-annex documents: the path MUST BE ABSOLUTE — a relative one resolves against the
      worktree top and is perturbed by GIT_WORK_TREE/core.worktree.
  (d) Avoid the index (plumbing): git-lfs's hot path (clean/smudge/filter-process) touches no index —
      a code search for index.lock across git-lfs/git-lfs returns ZERO hits; index use is confined to
      `git update-index -q --refresh` in git/git.go. Gerrit runs bare through JGit
      ObjectInserter/BatchRefUpdate, never a DirCache.
BEST-ARGUED STATEMENT OF THE PATTERN — git-annex prepareModifyIndex (Annex/Branch.hs L387-412),
which deletes any .git/annex/index.lock it finds, justified as: "Since all modifications of the index
are performed inside this module, and only when the journal is locked... no other process is
currently modifying the index. So any index.lock file must be stale."
=> THE LICENCE CONDITION for unlinking a git lock: OWN THE INDEX FILE EXCLUSIVELY **AND** HOLD YOUR
OWN LOCK OVER IT. Absent that, blind unlink is unsafe. lazygit's unconditional os.Remove and GitLab
Runner's delete-before-checkout are UI/CI shortcuts assuming single-writer.
NOTABLE NEGATIVE RESULTS — CITED: dulwich does exactly one O_EXCL open and converts FileExistsError
straight into FileLocked — no loop, no timeout, no staleness check (dulwich/file.py L168-283).
libgit2's filebuf.c lock_file() returns GIT_ELOCKED immediately with no retry and implements NONE of
git's ref-lock timeout semantics (filebuf.c L44-58) — so LIBGIT2-BASED TOOLS ARE MORE LOCK-FRAGILE
THAN THE C GIT CLI EVEN ON REFS. JGit's DirCache.lock() mirrors C git and does not retry the index.

== 2. TIMEOUTS ON PURELY LOCAL GIT SUBPROCESS CALLS — NO SETTLED ANSWER ==
CITED FOR: Gitaly bounds EVERY git command with a Go context deadline, in the same breath as raising
the lock timeouts — "context cancellation would still cause us to exit early in case the caller
doesn't want to wait this long". GitLab layers per-request Gitaly timeouts above that (MR 224510).
CITED AGAINST (the observed limit of the practice): where projects added git timeouts they scoped
them to NETWORK ops. Zuul's "Add git timeout" bounds remote clone/fetch at 300s and DELETES THE LOCAL
REPO on timeout, explicitly because GitPython's clone_from()/fetch() lack hard timeouts; local
operations untouched. GitPython's reported hangs (#547, #969) are clone/fetch. dulwich, libgit2,
git-lfs and git-annex bound NOTHING at the subprocess level.
EXTRAPOLATION — the honest synthesis: bounding a purely local git call is UNUSUAL IN APPLICATION CODE
AND STANDARD IN SERVER INFRASTRUCTURE. The dividing line is not local-vs-network, it is "IS THERE A
CALLER WITH A DEADLINE?" Gitaly has one (an RPC); a CLI does not.
  FOR: an unbounded local call can stall indefinitely on a stuck peer lock, a hung NFS/FUSE/network
  mount, or a wedged filesystem — and rebar's calls run WHILE HOLDING THE STORE WRITE LOCK, so one
  stall converts into a fleet-wide stall of every other agent. Failure without a bound is
  indistinguishable from slowness.
  AGAINST: a timeout can abort legitimately slow work (large gc, repack, cold-cache add on a huge
  tree) and, worse, can abort it MID-WRITE — which for git means leaving the very .lock files you
  were trying to avoid. Zuul's mitigation (delete and re-clone) is NOT available to rebar's tracker.
RECONCILABLE POSITION: a WATCHDOG-GRADE bound (generous, 2-10x worst legitimate case) is defensible;
a LATENCY-GRADE bound is not.

== 3. STALE-LOCK RECLAMATION: FOUR SCHEMES ==
THE DIRECT PRIOR ART — MERCURIAL — CITED. mercurial/lock.py already contains rebar's 304e fix:
  def _getlockprefix():
      """Return a string which is used to differentiate pid namespaces
      It's useful to detect "dead" processes and remove stale locks with confidence. Typically it's
      just hostname. On modern linux, we include an extra Linux-specific pid namespace identifier."""
      result = encoding.strtolocal(socket.gethostname())
      if pycompat.sysplatform.startswith(b'linux'):
          try: result += b'/%x' % os.stat(b'/proc/self/ns/pid').st_ino
          except (FileNotFoundError, PermissionError, NotADirectoryError): pass
      return result
FOUR DESIGN POINTS WORTH STEALING, same file:
 1. THE LOCK IS A SYMLINK WHOSE TARGET IS THE STAMP — creation and content are ONE ATOMIC STEP:
    "lock is symlink on platforms that support it, file on others. symlink is used because create of
    directory entry and contents are atomic even over nfs. old-style lock: symlink to pid.
    new-style lock: symlink to hostname:pid"
 2. BREAKING A STALE LOCK IS ITSELF DONE UNDER A SECOND LOCK. _testlock(): "if locker dead, break
    lock. must do this with another lock held, or can race and break valid lock" — takes <name>.break
    with timeout=0, RE-READS THE STAMP, and only then unlinks.
 3. FOREIGN PREFIX => NEVER BREAK (_lockshouldbebroken: if host != lock._host: return False).
 4. BOUNDED WAIT WITH A WARNING STAGE: lock() sleeps 1s per attempt down from ui.timeout, DEFAULT
    600s, with ui.timeout.warn (default 0) driving "waiting for lock on ... held by ..." and a
    "got lock after %d seconds" follow-up (configitems.toml).
WHAT MERCURIAL DOES NOT HAVE: no boot id, no process start-time qualification, NO AGE CEILING.
THE CONTAINER FAILURE MODE, BOTH DIRECTIONS — CITED:
 - rebar's direction (same host misread as foreign => orphan permanent): hostname is the container id
   and changes on recreate. rebar 5ef138d26 documents field data: 4f2e3e889406 -> 3790c7a6034a while
   boot id identical.
 - THE INVERSE, MORE DANGEROUS DIRECTION (foreign misread as stale => a LIVE lock broken):
   restic#4922 — running restic inside Flatpak, "when considering whether a lock from a restic
   process outside the container is stale or not, it (correctly) sees the same hostname but then
   can't see the pid and always decides the lock is stale." Same hostname, different PID namespace.
   THIS IS THE CASE rebar's `ns=` FIELD GUARDS.
 - boot_id IS GENUINELY HOST-WIDE, NOT NAMESPACED — the request to containerize it was closed
   WONTFIX, Lennart Poettering: "PID namespaces have many users, beyond systems which try to boot-up
   systems in them... Overmounting the boot id in userspace is very easy" (RH bug 854604).
   Consequences: (i) boot_id is the right host identity — CITED; (ii) trivially spoofable by an
   overmount and absent on non-Linux — CITED for mechanism, EXTRAPOLATION for risk.
COMPARISON:
 - pid + start-time: sound on one host+namespace. Footguns: starttime is clock-tick granular
   (/proc/pid/stat field 22); unavailable on macOS/Windows (degrades to bare pid); meaningless across
   pid namespaces. Kernel devs call starttime "useful to detect PID reuses in a somewhat reliable
   way" but tick-granular (LKML). filelock implements it: "A PID that no longer exists is gone; a
   live PID whose start token differs is a recycled PID".
 - KERNEL flock/fcntl: SOUNDEST — auto-released on death, no reclamation logic to get wrong.
   Footguns: advisory only; broken/absent on NFS; POSIX fcntl locks are LOST ON ANY close() of the
   fd, hence OFD locks. cargo SKIPS LOCKING ENTIRELY ON NFS because "the failure mode for flock on
   NFS is BLOCKING FOREVER, even if the 'non-blocking' flag is passed" (flock.rs). Bazel prefers OFD
   locks — "POSIX locks can be lost 'accidentally' due to any close() on the lock file, and are not
   reliably preserved across execve()" (blaze_util_posix.cc).
 - LEASE/TTL + HEARTBEAT: sound, and THE ONLY SCHEME THAT CANNOT WEDGE FOREVER. Footguns: needs clock
   sync; a paused/swapped holder can have its live lock stolen. restic: staleLockTimeout = 30min,
   refreshed every 5min, refreshabilityTimeout = staleLockTimeout - defaultRefreshInterval*3/2 "to
   compensate for a small time drift between clients". proper-lockfile (yarn 1): mkdir strategy,
   stale 10s, mtime heartbeat every stale/2, and it AVOIDS O_EXCL because "O_EXCL is broken on NFS
   file systems". flufl.lock has explicit lifetime + refresh.
 - BOOT-ID QUALIFICATION: sound for HOST identity, strictly better than hostname. Linux-only;
   spoofable by overmount; does NOT identify the namespace (needs the ns= companion).
THE HYBRID GIT ITSELF USES, THAT NOBODY NAMES: `git gc`'s gc.pid combines hostname + pid PLUS A
GENEROUS TTL BACKSTOP, in lock_repo_for_gc() (builtin/gc.c L718-778):
  /* 12 hour limit is very generous as gc should never take that long. On the other hand we don't
     really need a strict limit here, running gc --auto one day late is not a big problem. --force
     can be used in manual gc after the user verifies that no gc is running. */
  time(NULL) - st.st_mtime <= 12 * 3600 &&
  fscanf(fp, scan_fmt, &pid, locking_host) == 2 &&
  /* be gentle to concurrent "gc" on remote hosts */
  (strcmp(locking_host, my_host) || !kill(pid, 0) || errno == EPERM);
READ CAREFULLY: a FOREIGN HOST'S STAMP IS UNCONDITIONALLY RESPECTED (the conservative rule rebar
shares) — BUT the 12-hour mtime ceiling means it can never wedge the repository FOREVER.
*** THAT COMBINATION IS THE PIECE REBAR IS MISSING. ***
Yarn Berry states the asymmetry that makes liveness probes safe: "It's not foolproof (there are false
positive), but there are no false negative and that's all that matters in 99% of the cases" — a false
"alive" makes you wait (safe); a false "dead" makes you break a live lock (corruption).
Bazel's rule is the cleanest risk-elimination: it writes pid/owner/cwd/tty into the lock and comments
"The contents are printed for human consumption when another client fails to take the lock, but not
parsed otherwise" — ALL THE DIAGNOSTIC VALUE OF AN OWNER STAMP, ZERO PID-REUSE EXPOSURE, because the
kernel lock is the only authority.

== 4. BLOCKING POLICY UNDER CONTENTION, AND THE STARTUP CASE ==
WHAT MATURE TOOLS DO — CITED:
 cargo package cache: try_lock then KERNEL-BLOCK FOREVER; prints "Blocking waiting for file lock on
   package cache" once. No timeout.
 Bazel client: 500ms poll loop FOREVER; prints owner dump then "Waiting for it to complete...";
   --noblock_for_lock => exit LOCK_HELD_NOBLOCK_FOR_LOCK. NO --lock_timeout EXISTS (0 code hits).
 Bazel server: commandLock.wait(500) loop forever; LockingMode.ERROR_OUT escape.
 Mercurial: 1s poll to ui.timeout = 600s, with a warn stage; timeout=0 escape.
 Python filelock: poll, timeout=-1 = forever; multi-file backends use JITTERED EXPONENTIAL BACKOFF
   with secrets.randbelow; timeout=0 = one attempt.
 portalocker: BOUNDED — DEFAULT_TIMEOUT = 5s, DEFAULT_CHECK_INTERVAL = 0.25s, then raise.
 yarn 1: 200ms poll FOREVER, --mutex opt-in. yarn berry: 16.7ms poll, HARD 60s then throw.
 pnpm: NO STORE LOCK AT ALL. git (ref locks): jittered quadratic backoff to a config'd budget.
 git gc --auto: FAIL FAST, SILENTLY.
PNPM'S ANSWER IS THE MOST RADICAL AND IT WORKS. zkochan, pnpm discussion #10702: "It is safe to run
multiple installs concurrently, which modify the same store. All store related operations are atomic.
The store will never be left in a broken state. The store is not locked. When multiple installers use
the same store, they might redundantly download and extract the same package multiple times but it
will work." Contention DESIGNED OUT via atomic rename-based writes; the trade is redundant work.
(Could not confirm the PR that removed the old directory locking — "pnpm v6" is UNVERIFIED.)
NO SETTLED ANSWER: block-forever (cargo, Bazel, yarn 1) and bounded (portalocker, berry, Mercurial,
git) are both mainstream. Near-universal among block-forever: A VISIBLE, REPEATED WAITING MESSAGE
NAMING THE HOLDER. Near-universal among bounded: JITTER.
THE STARTUP CASE — CITED. Git's own answer to "a background/implicit path wants a lock" is FAIL FAST,
SILENTLY (builtin/gc.c L992-1001):
  name = lock_repo_for_gc(force, &pid);
  if (name) {
          if (opts.auto_flag) { ret = 0; goto out; /* be quiet on --auto */ }
          die(_("gc is already running on machine '%s' pid %"PRIuMAX" (use --force if not)"), ...);
  }
An EXPLICIT `git gc` dies loudly with the holder's host and pid. The IMPLICIT --auto path — the one on
every user's hot path, EXACTLY ANALOGOUS TO REBAR'S BOOT ENSURE SWEEP — returns success and does
nothing. Housekeeping is opportunistic; it never blocks the thing the user asked for.
Bazel's --noblock_for_lock docs make the same point for automation: "Developers might use this in
presubmit checks to avoid long waits caused by another Bazel command in the same client."
EXTRAPOLATION — the general rule: THE ACQUISITION BUDGET MUST BE STRICTLY SMALLER THAN THE DEADLINE OF
WHOEVER IS WAITING ON YOU. rebar's incident was a 60s budget under a 30s health check — a
straightforward violation. COROLLARY THAT MATTERS MORE: fail-fast on a startup path must be LOUD IN
TELEMETRY AND IDEMPOTENTLY RETRIED LATER, or you have converted a stall into silent skipped work.

== 5. RECOMMENDATIONS FOR REBAR ==
5a. DOES THE TWO-LEG flock+mkdir DESIGN MATCH, EXCEED, OR FALL SHORT?
It EXCEEDS mature practice on soundness of reclamation and FALLS SHORT on liveness guarantees.
WHERE IT EXCEEDS (EXTRAPOLATION grounded in the cited comparisons):
 - The fcntl leg gives the kernel-mediated auto-release property cargo and Bazel rely on. The mkdir
   leg gives the portable second window and NFS tolerance flock lacks. Neither leg waits on the other
   across processes, so no deadlock. VERY FEW PROJECTS RUN BOTH.
 - The 304e stamp (rebar-lock v2 host=<boot-id|name> ns=<pidns-inode> pid=<pid> start=<starttime>) is
   STRICTLY STRONGER THAN MERCURIAL'S hostname/nsinode:pid — it adds boot-id host identity and
   start-time pid qualification, NEITHER OF WHICH MERCURIAL HAS.
 - The "reclaim only under the fcntl proof" rule for the cross-namespace case is GENUINELY NOVEL and,
   as far as the researcher could tell, correct. NO PRIOR ART FOUND DOING THIS. Sounder than the
   alternatives (mtime heuristic, or refusing forever).
 - rebar's colon-free v2 stamp, deliberately unparseable to an older reader, is BETTER
   FORWARD-COMPATIBILITY HYGIENE than anything in the surveyed projects.
WHERE IT FALLS SHORT:
 1. NO AGE CEILING ANYWHERE. git gc has 12h, restic 30min, proper-lockfile 10s, flufl.lock a lifetime.
    rebar has none. EVERY "refuse without proof" branch — absent stamp, malformed stamp, foreign host
    identity — WEDGES THE STORE PERMANENTLY. That is the CLASS of the 304e incident; 304e fixed one
    instance (the container-recreate identity) and LEFT THE CLASS OPEN.
 2. NO JITTER. _acquire_fcntl sleeps a fixed 50ms, _acquire_mkdir a fixed 100ms, and
    gitutil._with_index_lock_retry a linear 0.2 x attempt. Git jitters +-25% SPECIFICALLY to
    de-synchronize competing processes. With many agents this is a THUNDERING HERD.
 3. NO HOLDER DISCLOSURE TO THE WAITER. cargo, Bazel, Mercurial and yarn all tell the user who holds
    the lock and that they are waiting. rebar waits SILENTLY for up to 60s then reports only a
    duration. Bazel's "print it, never parse it" is free to adopt.
5b. SHOULD LOCAL-ONLY GIT CALL SITES BE BOUNDED? YES, BUT AS A WATCHDOG, NOT A LATENCY BUDGET.
 1. SET GIT'S THREE LOCK KNOBS ON EVERY INVOCATION — highest value per unit risk, and the only
    fully cited-precedent move (Gitaly). Add
    `-c core.filesRefLockTimeout=1000 -c core.packedRefsTimeout=10000 -c core.configLockTimeout=10000`
    to the module-local _git helpers. Bounds HEAD.lock / packed-refs.lock / config.lock contention
    INSIDE GIT where it belongs, and costs nothing when uncontended.
 2. ADD A GENEROUS subprocess.run(..., timeout=...) WATCHDOG — 120s for ordinary plumbing, higher for
    compact/fsck/gc-adjacent work. rebar's calls run WHILE HOLDING THE STORE WRITE LOCK, so an
    unbounded stall on a hung mount converts one process's problem into every agent's — precisely the
    coupling Gitaly's context deadlines prevent. Keep it well above any legitimate duration; the goal
    is to distinguish "wedged" from "slow". EXTRAPOLATION: treat a timeout as a HARD FAULT (surface
    it, release the lock) rather than retrying — an aborted git write is exactly what leaves .lock
    residue.
 3. DO NOT BOUND metrics/blame.py and metrics/git_metrics.py TIGHTLY. git blame and log walks over a
    long-lived tickets branch are legitimately slow and hold NO store lock; a low bound would produce
    spurious `unavailable` metrics. A high watchdog (e.g. 300s) is fine.
 4. ADD JITTER to _acquire_fcntl (50ms), _acquire_mkdir (100ms) and gitutil._with_index_lock_retry
    (0.2 x attempt). Copy git's shape: multiply each sleep by uniform [0.75, 1.25].
 5. ADD AN AGE CEILING to _mkdir_lock_is_stale for the refuse-without-proof branches, following
    git gc's 12-hour precedent. Choose far above any legitimate hold (the write lock is held for a
    single event append — seconds), e.g. 1 hour. Preserves yaw-gravel-linen conservatism in the
    normal case while REMOVING THE PERMANENT-WEDGE FAILURE CLASS ENTIRELY.
    *** SINGLE HIGHEST-VALUE CHANGE, FULLY BACKED BY PRIOR ART. ***
 6. GIVE THE BOOT PATH GIT'S --auto SEMANTICS. mcp_server.py:705 already passes timeout=5,
    attempts=1 — good, consistent with gc --auto. But run_ensures logs LockTimeout at warning and
    returns silently. Make the skip OBSERVABLE AND RE-ATTEMPTED: a metric/telemetry counter plus a
    later opportunistic retry, so a permanently-contended store cannot silently never run its ensure
    units.
5c. FOOTGUNS THE TWO INCIDENTS DID NOT SURFACE:
 1. THE mkdir -> OWNER-STAMP WRITE IS NOT ATOMIC, AND THE GAP WEDGES FOREVER. _acquire_mkdir does
    os.mkdir(lock_dir) THEN opens and writes `owner`; the write is best-effort inside a bare
    `except OSError: pass`. If the process dies in that window — or the stamp write fails —
    _mkdir_lock_is_stale hits decision rule 1 (owner absent/unreadable => False) and the lock is
    PERMANENTLY UNRECLAIMABLE, by exactly the 304e mechanism. The docstring acknowledges the window
    and declines to act. MERCURIAL DESIGNED THIS OUT: the lock IS a symlink whose target is the stamp,
    "because create of directory entry and contents are atomic even over nfs". An age ceiling (rec 5)
    closes this too; a symlink lock closes it properly.
 2. RECLAMATION DOES NOT RE-VERIFY UNDER THE BREAK LOCK. _acquire_mkdir calls _mkdir_lock_is_stale()
    then _reclaim_mkdir_lock() as two separate steps. Mercurial's _testlock takes a SECOND lock
    (<name>.break), RE-READS the stamp, and re-checks before unlinking, warning "must do this with
    another lock held, or can race and break valid lock." rebar's fcntl leg serializes Python
    acquirers, covering the common case — but bash-era locks and dual_window=False callers exist, and
    any writer taking the mkdir leg without the fcntl leg is outside that protection.
    EXTRAPOLATION: low probability, HIGH SEVERITY (breaking a live lock => concurrent store writes).
 3. LockHandle.release() UNLINKS UNCONDITIONALLY — removes `owner` and rmdirs without verifying the
    stamp is still ours. If a peer ever did mis-reclaim (footgun 2), release would then delete that
    peer's FRESH lock, cascading one misclassification into two. Mercurial guards release with
    `if self._getpid() != self.pid: return`. Checking the stamp before unlink is a two-line hardening.
 4. ON macOS THE v2 STAMP SILENTLY DEGRADES to hostname + bare pid. _read_boot_id,
    _read_pid_namespace_id and _process_start_time all read /proc and all return None on Darwin, so
    the stamp becomes host=name-<hostname> ns=- pid=<n> start=-. Decision rule 5 treats "both unknown"
    as COMPARABLE, so it probes the pid WITH NO START-TIME QUALIFICATION. Given many concurrent local
    agents and macOS as the operator's platform, THE PID-REUSE DEFENCE 304e ADDED IS NOT ACTIVE ON THE
    PLATFORM WHERE CONCURRENCY IS HIGHEST. psutil.Process(pid).create_time() or `ps -o lstart= -p`
    would restore it. CITED for the mechanism; EXTRAPOLATION for the exposure.
 5. TWO MACS SHARING A FILESYSTEM WITH THE SAME DEFAULT HOSTNAME COLLIDE. With no boot id,
    _host_identity() is name-<hostname>; macOS defaults are non-unique (MacBook-Pro.local). Two such
    hosts on a shared volume would each judge the other's stamp "same host" and probe a meaningless
    local pid — the restic#4922 hazard in its DANGEROUS direction (breaking a LIVE foreign lock).
    EXTRAPOLATION, but the ingredients are cited.
 6. run_ensures SWALLOWING LockTimeout IS A CORRECTNESS RISK, NOT JUST LATENCY. On a permanently
    contended store the ensure sweep never runs and the only trace is a logger.warning. The migration
    registry is idempotent, so a SKIPPED sweep is safe — but a NEVER-RUN sweep means the store
    silently drifts from the schema every code path assumes. gc --auto gets away with this posture
    because gc is pure housekeeping; MIGRATIONS ARE NOT. Needs a counter and an eventual forced sweep.
 7. gitutil'S index.lock RECLAMATION IS MTIME-ONLY. _INDEX_LOCK_STALE_S = 300 with no pid or owner
    check — the WEAKEST scheme in the survey (yarn 1 / proper-lockfile's model but WITHOUT
    proper-lockfile's compensating heartbeat that keeps a live holder's mtime fresh). Git never
    refreshes index.lock's mtime, so any git op legitimately holding the index >300s (a big repack, a
    slow add on a cold FUSE mount) HAS ITS LOCK UNLINKED UNDERNEATH IT. git-annex's licence condition
    is the standard rebar would need to meet, and it requires OWNING THE INDEX: see footgun 8.
 8. REBAR DOES NOT USE GIT_INDEX_FILE ISOLATION, AND IT IS THE OBVIOUS FIT. The tracker worktree's
    .git/index is shared with anything else touching that worktree. Both git-annex (.git/annex/index
    via withIndexFile) and git itself (stash, filter-branch) point their own operations at a private
    index file. rebar's event-append path is a small closed set of stages — a dedicated ABSOLUTE-PATH
    GIT_INDEX_FILE would (a) eliminate index.lock contention with foreign writers outright, and
    (b) RETROACTIVELY LICENSE the mtime reclamation in footgun 7, because rebar would then be the
    provable sole owner. EXTRAPOLATION for rebar; CITED as the pattern.
 9. _reclaim_mkdir_lock AND THE STAMP WRITE BOTH SWALLOW EVERY OSError. A read-only or full
    filesystem, or a permissions problem, degrades silently into "the lock can never be reclaimed"
    with no diagnostic. Compare _acquire_fcntl, which rebar recently and correctly hardened (commit
    7b858c1a3, "discriminate contention from real faults") — the same discrimination has NOT been
    applied to the mkdir leg.
10. NON-ISSUE, VERIFIED — recorded so a future session does not re-litigate it: the fcntl fd is
    created with os.open(lock_path, os.O_CREAT | os.O_RDWR) with no O_CLOEXEC, which would normally
    risk leaking the lock into a long-lived child. PEP 446 makes Python-created fds non-inheritable by
    default; confirmed os.get_inheritable(fd) is False on this interpreter. THE SAFETY IS REAL BUT
    IMPLICIT — worth an inline comment, since explicit O_CLOEXEC costs nothing and git states the
    property deliberately ("the file descriptor returned by hold_lock_file_for_update() is marked
    O_CLOEXEC", lockfile.h).
5d. PRIORITY ORDERING (coordinator note: item 2 below is ALREADY DONE — see the correction at top):
 1. Age ceiling on all refuse-without-proof branches — git gc 12h / restic 30min / flufl lifetime.
    Risk if skipped: PERMANENT STORE WEDGE — the 304e failure class, still open.
 2. [ALREADY DONE — 5ef138d26 is on origin/main] Land fix-304e-container-lock on main.
 3. Set the three core.*Timeout knobs on every git invocation — Gitaly. Risk: avoidable ref/config
    lock failures under agent storms.
 4. Jitter every retry sleep — git lockfile.c, filelock. Risk: thundering herd at high agent counts.
 5. Watchdog timeout= on local git subprocesses — Gitaly context deadlines. Risk: one hung mount
    stalls every agent.
 6. Start-time qualification on macOS (psutil/ps fallback) — filelock, LKML. Risk: pid-reuse defence
    absent on the highest-concurrency platform.
 7. Atomic stamp (symlink lock) or re-verify under a break lock — Mercurial lock.py. Risk:
    crash-in-window => permanent wedge; live-lock break.
 8. Report the holder to the waiter (print, never parse) — Bazel, Mercurial, cargo. Risk: 60s of
    silence is indistinguishable from a hang.
 9. GIT_INDEX_FILE isolation for the event-append path — git-annex, git stash. Risk: index.lock
    contention; unlicensed mtime reclamation.
10. Make the run_ensures skip observable + eventually forced — gc --auto precedent, but migrations
    are not housekeeping. Risk: silent schema drift on a busy store.
